rv.q: Although it’s early days for theatre-going in 2024, there’s a real feeling of “at last!” about Beth Steel’s new play. At the National, playwrights haven’t always been on-song of late. And more widely there has been a concerning dearth of entertaining new writing that also matters.

Her family can’t hide their mixed feelings about her Polish husband-to-be Marek (Marc Wootton). Her dad John (Derek Riddell) forgets his name in his after-dinner speech, protesting that he hardly knows him, while her sister Hazel (Lucy Black) makes snide comments about migrants taking the best jobs in their opportunity-starved former mining town.

The texture of her writing – her salty wit and her sure, compassionate touch with the subtleties of intimate interaction, especially between women – unfailingly absorbs and compels. And Bijan Sheibani’s production, performed with terrific verve by a crack cast, sears and scintillates.

Since none of his own relations is present, he is very much the outsider. Although he serenades Sylvia with a cornily romantic but touching song, disharmony lurks beneath the disco glitterball. Sylvia’s abrasive sister Hazel (Lucy Black) resents the growing presence of eastern Europeans in the town.
Nevertheless, while the wedding might be a disaster, the show is a triumph.
